steps.observation: You have 300 seconds. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptual tour of a Transformer

1. Goal  
   We want a model that can understand a whole sequence (a sentence, paragraph, code, music, …) and decide, for every element, which other elements matter and by how much. That “who-cares-about-whom” map is called attention.

2. Input becomes vectors  
   • Tokenisation: break text into pieces (words, sub-words).  
   • Embedding: look up each token in a table → a vector (e.g., 768 numbers).  
   • Positional encoding: add or concatenate a position-dependent pattern so the model knows order (because attention itself is position-agnostic).

3. Self-attention: the core trick  
   For every token we create three small vectors by multiplying the embedding with learned matrices:  
   • Query (Q): “What am I looking for?”  
   • Key (K): “What do I offer?”  
   • Value (V): “What information do I carry?”

   Think of standing in a room: your Query asks questions; everyone else holds up Keys; you measure how well your Query matches each Key (dot product). The better the match, the more you listen to that person’s Value. Softmax turns the scores into weights that sum to 1. Weighted averaging of all Values gives a new representation of the current token—one that already mixes in information from the whole sequence.

4. Multi-head attention  
   Instead of doing this once, we do it in parallel “heads” (e.g., 12). Each head has its own Q, K, V matrices, so one head might focus on subject–verb agreement, another on coreference, etc. Heads are concatenated and projected back to the model dimension.

5. Add & Norm + Feed-Forward  
   After attention:  
   • Add residual connection (original input + attention output)  
   • Layer Normalisation (stabilises training)  
   • Position-wise Feed-Forward Network (two linear layers with a non-linearity, applied to each position separately)  
   • Another Add & Norm

6. Stack it  
   A “layer” = Multi-head Attention + FFN + residuals/norms. Transformers use many layers (12, 24, 96 …). Depth lets the model perform progressively richer mixing and abstraction.

7. Encoder vs. Decoder  
   Original paper (for translation) used:  
   • Encoder: full self-attention (each token sees all others).  
   • Decoder: masked self-attention (token can’t peek at future tokens) + encoder–decoder attention (decoder tokens attend to encoder outputs).  
   GPT-style models keep only the masked decoder; BERT keeps only the encoder (unmasked) and is trained with masked-token prediction.

8. Training objective  
   Choose an objective that produces gradients: cross-entropy for next-token prediction, masked-token recovery, etc. Optimiser (Adam) nudges the Q/K/V/FFN weights so that the attention patterns and transformations improve the objective.

9. Inference (text generation)  
   Feed past tokens, compute masked self-attention, get probability distribution for next token, sample/beam-search, append, repeat.

Why it’s powerful  
• Attention lets any token reach any other in one step (no vanishing-gradient bottleneck of RNNs).  
• Parallelisable: all tokens processed simultaneously on GPUs/TPUs.  
• Scaling laws: more layers, heads, data keep improving performance.

In one sentence: A Transformer continuously asks, for every word, “whom should I pay attention to right now?”, uses those choices to mix information across the sequence through multi-head attention, repeats the process in deep layers, and learns the attention patterns and mixing functions end-to-end from data.
